utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, everybody. Mr. Registrar, will you please tell us which case this is? First, I should like to say good afternoon to the interpreters. I hope they can hear me, all the booths. Good afternoon. Also good afternoon to all the parties present here and the accused. Now I should also like to ask Mr. Nice to take the floor and tell us now what it is that the Judges have to hear from you regarding your case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are in the closing stages of the Prosecution case. There are two substantive witnesses remaining: the witness who deals with the interviews of the defendant, and the Witness John Ralston who deals with a number of matters and who will come at the end. First, there's an argument on admissibility that my learned friend, Mr. Greaves, wishes to raise in relation to photographs. There are small bundles of the proposed photographs available for you, and I hope they've been provided -- oh, they're coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As this is a matter of admissibility, I should ask that the session be temporarily private because, of course, if you rule the documents inadmissible, it would be inappropriate for the public to have heard about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, a private session. Yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Nice, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The photographs can be agreed for what they are, in light of the ruling, or they can be produced by one witness who I am calling in any event, and Mr. Basham, if that becomes necessary. I'll return to those later, having discussed the matter with Mr. Greaves. We turn to the interviews. The interviews have presented a difficulty as to how they should be presented. Before I come to that and explain what I'm proposing, I should say that Mr. Basham, pursuant to the Court's order, is in court as the officer or the investigator dealing with the case, but he is one of the two investigators who was present at the interviews of the defendant, and it may be, if there's anything contentious in the interviews, that it would be appropriate for him to withdraw now, before the officer who is going to give evidence of the interviews comes in. On the other hand, if there's nothing contentious known to my learned friend that's going to arise in the cross-examination, I would ask that he be allowed to stay, because he is the continuing investigator in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Although for no particular reason, I think it would be better, just in case anything should arise unexpectedly, that he should go out in any event, rather than there being any specific reason for it. One knows that sometimes things can happen that are unexpected. It's really just a safety-first issue really, I think, that I'm raising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm entirely in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Basham should go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court has been provided with bundles of the interviews separated out as to the dates of the individual interviews and, so far as the President's copy of the interviews is concerned, marked with green and blue tags. The only reason that Judge Riad's and Judge Rodrigues' versions haven't been similarly marked is simply want of time. Those tags represent, in total, the pages that the Prosecution and Defence, in combination -- I trust you have one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very sorry, Mr. Nice, but the Judges, who do not quite know the programme, wish that they could have -- it was said last week we were given these folders, but I believe that we should try to find these documents for the Judges, or perhaps we should adjourn for a couple of minutes until the Judges are provided with this folder. Mr. Nice, I think that would be better. Yes, it is quite true that you provided a very complete document, but we did not know that this afternoon we would be dealing with this folder, so I think we should adjourn. I shall ask my secretary to look for these documents, but perhaps it would be faster if I go there. Excuse me for this short misunderstanding. We shall make a very brief adjournment, and as good pupils, we shall have with us all the aids, and then we shall be able to proceed. Thank you very much. So I shall go and look for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. We are now ready because we now have all the documents with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I trust that you have the version that has the green and blue stickers down the side, and those reveal what it was originally the intention of both parties collectively to have presented to you in detail. Green represents a place to start in the interview and blue represents a place to stop. I have added up, with the officer who's going to deal with these interviews, how long it would take to read all those passages out in English at a reasonably slow speed, and my forecast is that it would take longer than you like, considerably; probably five hours, something like that. What I propose, and I hope this is acceptable to you, is to call the officer, to get him to give a summary of the interviews that took place and the setting in which they took place, to make some summarising remarks about features of the interview and then to get him to deal, first, in an entirely summary way, with the very first interview, which has got no stickers, blue or green, on it, to deal reasonably extensively with the passages marked by the green and blue stickers in the first interview of the 4th of June, because that covers a lot of important matters and will be of value to the Chamber, and it may be that there will come a time when we will be able to review whether the Chamber wishes the exercise of the reading in detail to be continued and completed, or whether it may be possible to deal with things in some other more summary way. Can I say that I've had a request from the Defence that there may be private sessions for -- it's not for me to say. They've asked that I should ask for private sessions for certain passages of the evidence, and there would be reasons for our seeking private sessions for certain passages of the evidence. Can I suggest, with that in mind, that we don't lay the document on the ELMO, because all too possibly the relevant names or facts that would be the subject of an application to hold a private session would be displayed to the public before anybody picked on the point and had gone into private session? So can I ask that they're simply dealt with by the officer having the volume in front of him and read out by him? If that seems to be an acceptable way to go ahead, then I'd ask for the officer to be called in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections? Let us have the witness brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please give us your full name, the date of your birth, your current occupation, and then you will take the solemn declaration, and I will say no more at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my full name is Bernard Patrick O'Donnell. My date of birth is the 16th of September, 1962, and I am an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you now make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. O'Donnell. You may be seated. You are called by the Prosecution. Will you please sit down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not need to explain to you the procedure because you all know it, and I will now give the floor to the Prosecution and then to the Defence. Mr. Nice? Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, were you for some time the investigator dealing with this case and effectively in charge of it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently relinquish that responsibility to Mr. Basham, you turning your attention to other cases?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in the role you held and, indeed, later on, I think, when Mr. Basham had already arrived, did you conduct some interviews with the defendant, Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct. Your Honours, we conducted a series of interviews with Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you produce -- and I think it's already been given a number -- a binder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice and the witness, will you please slow down? I do not know whether you will speak faster than this or not, but will you please bear in mind that the interpreters have also to do their work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters for forgetting that we're speaking in the same language and, therefore, fall foul of the temptation to go too fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interviews, Mr. O'Donnell -- I can't remember how many in all, but there were several of them -- were conducted over what overall period of time?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The first interview was conducted on the 25th of February, 1998, there were in total nine interviews conducted, and the last interview was conducted on the 24th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they conducted?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: They were conducted here at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we turn to the detail or even the summary of any of these interviews, can you help the Chamber in relation to cooperation of the defendant? First, is it the case that the Office of the Prosecutor has said from time to time that it will report on cooperation of the defendant to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I would like to make a couple of points on cooperation. Firstly, Mr. Jelisic took part in a total of nine formal interviews. He voluntarily took part in those interviews, some of which were quite lengthy. In total, approximately 25 to 30 hours of interviews were recorded on videotape. During the interviews, he gave information about crimes and admitted to the crimes -- to the individual murders, and he also gave information about other matters. To that extent, he cooperated. I cannot say, though, that he fully cooperated. He was very definite about the matters that he would talk about and when. It was, at times, difficult to get specific information from him, and he often became agitated when asked for further information or where inconsistencies were highlighted. Whilst Mr. Jelisic gave us information about the crimes, he presented us with what I believe is a very sanitised version of events, very different to information that was given to us by witnesses and inconsistent in itself. A lot of what Mr. Jelisic told us is not believable. I believe that Mr. Jelisic used the interviews as an opportunity to present his actions in the best possible light.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time -- I'm sorry. We'll leave a break, which we must do, between question and answer. At the time of these interviews, had witness statements been served on the Defence?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, they had. A number of witness statements had been given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the defendant agree, at any stage, to be interviewed about the charge of genocide?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: He did agree that there would be interviews on genocide, but the agreement was that we would cover the individual murders first and then move on to discussion on the crime of genocide. And at that point, we intended to put to him a number of inconsistencies in his story, along with inconsistencies between the story that he gave us and that told to us by witnesses. However, before we could do that, I was advised by Mr. Jelisic that he would no longer take part in the interviews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, on the topic of information provided by him touching on other people, without any names being given, what value, if any, was that information provided by him?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic gave us other information apart from information relating just to his crimes. The information that he gave is of limited use, firstly because it is not information, in the most part, which was new to us, and, secondly, because of the number of inconsistencies in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On inconsistencies, because the Chamber may not go through the totality of the interviews through you, as a witness, what particular topics were there in respect of which he gave differing accounts?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: There are a number of broad areas that there are inconsistencies in his version of events. Mr. Jelisic claimed that he was forced to commit the murders that he did and that he killed people, fearing that if he did not, then he himself would be killed. He claimed that he stayed in Brcko because he was told to, and again he feared that if he disobeyed orders, he would have been killed. He claimed that he only killed people that he was told to and that he never killed anyone of his own free will. In fact, he said that where he had the opportunity of not killing someone, then he didn't kill them, and he saw that as a personal triumph. There are a number of inconsistencies in his claims on those points, and I believe that his claims are not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a sense, your belief on the matter is not to the point; it's just identifying the different stories.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: There are a number of inconsistencies on those points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also give an account of the reasons for leaving Brcko, and was that one that was always the same or not?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: There are differences in his version of events and, again, inconsistencies in his claim that he had to stay in Brcko. Would you like me to go on with --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I think that's enough, by way of a headline, for the Chamber, and we'll now move, please, to the interviews themselves. The first one was on the 25th/26th of February. On this occasion, you were accompanied by whom as interviewer?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The interview on the 25th of February was with myself and Investigator Martina Fietz.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those names can be found on page 1 of this interview, and we do not propose to lead matters in detail from this interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. O'Donnell, summarise, and really summarise quite shortly, what was covered in this interview, should the Chamber want to look at it in detail at a later stage or at any stage?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The interview on the 25th of February, along with the interview on the 26th of February, covered the background of Mr. Jelisic -- his childhood, his upbringing and his education -- in great detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give any explanation for how he came to be involved in the things alleged against him?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic told of the illness suffered by his mother when he was very young, the limited time that he spent with his father, the death of his grandmother, and sickness in his childhood which he said initially led to him being not a good student. Later, in early high school, he said he associated with, as he put it, bad friends -- smoking, and he started drinking alcohol. Later, he was married and separated from his wife, a point he said caused him a lot of sadness, and he said that he began to spend enormous amounts of money in different bars, ordering sad songs because of the woman who left him, and this led him to become involved in criminal activity, being fraud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a matter of detail for the Chamber to have in mind. At the time of or shortly before these events, had he, as is revealed in the interviews, been before the courts locally?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a prison sentence imposed or not?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: A prison sentence was imposed. He appealed that sentence, and the sentence was later confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He makes reference to that in the course of the interviews?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn to the interview of the 4th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to deal with some of this in detail, and I hope that the speed I am speaking at is acceptable to the interpreters. If not, I'm sure I will be corrected. One way of dealing with interviews of this sort, to assist the Tribunal and to make them a little less difficult to consume, is for me to read the answers of the defendant, for the officer to read the questions of the interrogators; and provided we do that at a sensible speed, it's not then necessary for us regularly to say, "Did he say this?" and "Did you say that?" So if that course is acceptable to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, of course it is agreeable. But you really deem it necessary to read the whole interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I've indicated, although in this first interview I will read quite a lot of the marked passages indicated by the green and blue markers, I think by the second interview and certainly by the later interviews, it will be necessary to read or to take you to other smaller portions. But the first interview, I think, does contain a lot of material that will be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we turn to the interview of the 4th of June, Mr. O'Donnell, page 1 shows the people present, and between pages 1 to 4, the detailed preparations for the interview and the careful establishment of consent and so on is gone through; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 5, and I trust that -- just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that the booths all have copies. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, are you paying attention? For the record, you have to mention the pages and also the counts. And the document, is it also mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was distributed already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you write numbers from 1 to 17, and each one of them corresponds to one of the fragments?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So it is 66, this is Exhibit 66, and it goes from 1 to 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Now, excuse me. No, it goes from 1 to 14. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I discover that a small technical problem has developed, in that the versions of the interviews provided to the interpreters' booths on Friday may have been mislaid. Ms. Reynders, our ever-helpful case manager, is going to see what happened to them, because they were provided last week. But if it's acceptable to the booths, I'll carry on speaking at this sort of speed until they are found.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth has its copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 5 then, please, and if you would like to pick it up with the first question by you.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: On line 4; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I said, "Let's start with your arrival in Brcko. Can you tell me when you arrived in Brcko, please?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I arrived in Brcko on the last day of April '92, so I don't know it was 30th of April or 31st of April. I don't know how many days April has, but the last day of April."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Why did you go to Brcko?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I was brought to Brcko. Now I don't know how to explain this. First we were gathered by TO members, TO members of the Bijeljina TO. We were gathered in front of the TO building in Bijeljina. You can ask questions."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. Can you give me some background to how that came about, how you came to go to Brcko with the TO, please?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "On that day, around noon, we were at a funeral in the village of Brodac near Bijeljina. It was the funeral of Alexander Sasapopovic, who had committed suicide by shooting himself from a handgun. At the funeral were present some young men, a group of young men that I knew from Bijeljina. Out of that group, a young man whom I knew called me and said that Major Blogoje Gavrilovic was there, Major, and that he had something to offer, some kind of deal. When I approached the group, when I approached the group, Gavrilovic told me to be in front of the TO building at 4.00 p.m. in civilian clothes and to have my uniform in a plastic bag. Already there I learned that there was a plan that they were not -- that they were going to go to Brcko and that there were not many Serbs in Brcko, and that's why a group from Bijeljina had to go there. Sometime before 4.00, I arrived in front of the TO building in Bijeljina, where there were roughly 25 young men that I knew from before, most of them. We were told that we would be transported in civilian vehicles to the sugar-processing plant in Obaska near Bijeljina. In the administration building of this factory, of this plant, there was a reconnaissance unit stationed whose commander was precisely this Major Gavrilovic. We arrived in two four-wheel drives, Russian, Lada Niva, and there was one ordinary Lada and one ordinary Zastava 101 car. These two vehicles, Lada Niva were property of the TO in the Bijelina TO. When we gathered at the sugar processing plant, there were more soldiers in camouflaged uniforms. We were then told why we were going to Brcko, what we would do there and what the definitive object of our going there was. We were then told briefly that on the 1st of May, in the morning, the bridge would be blown up and that after that the war would start and that we would be given further instructions in the Serbian Orthodox Church in Brcko where Crisis Staff of Brcko would meet us; of the municipality of Brcko would meet us. I don't exactly know what time it was when we set off, but I believe that we arrived roughly around 8.00 to the -- in the Serbian Orthodox Church, which is the Srpska Varos Serbian part of Brcko. When we arrived in front of the church, the entrance, we saw there roughly 70 men in uniform. Ninety, sorry, mistake seventy armed men about 90 per cent of them were in civilian clothes."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for what follows, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But to avoid this coming and going from and into private sessions, I should -- because we all have the text in front of us, and when you say -- instead of saying "family so-and-so," perhaps you could say "family X" or "family Y," because it is simpler perhaps than constantly switching in and out of private sessions. If you have a whole passage which concerns a particular family, then we shall go into private session. I'm simply trying to simplify matters as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. I will pursue that course and probably miss out nearly all names on one side or the other, and that will save time, I think, as well. I pick it up at the top of page 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "There were several lists because there were several formations. Already people had arrived from Serbia and what I had heard is that many people who had been on this list had already been killed a day or two before the war had started at night in their homes."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. You said that the people on the list were, as they were referred to 'Ustasha,' and others had put up people in the town, were there any other people on the lists?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "People who financed and people who procured weapons for them. People who knew in advance what was going to happen."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Were there any others mentioned such as politicians, academics, business figures?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Yes, I was given a list myself; and yes these were prominent people, that's the only way to describe them."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "How many people were on the list that you were given?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Twenty to twenty-three, twenty-five maximum."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Were they all men or were they men and women?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "On the list there were only men. On my list there were only men."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Who gave you that list?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Yes, we'll go on to that question. That night when we arrived I was not then given a list, we were just shown a list and they were then mentioning certain families that were considered to be the most extremist. We were told about the Ljuca family. For instance here, who's a witness for the prosecution ..." I'll leave a [blank]. If this is acceptable, if I use the word "[blank]" whenever I miss a name out, it may be easier to follow because if we start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just do not mention the surname. Just do not mention names, if you can avoid that. Of course, if there is a dispute, if it is a matter for contention, then we shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "For instance here, who's a witness for the Prosecution, [blank], who was supposed to be killed. Families Ramic --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "-- and Bukvic, these were the most wanted families as far as I remember."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Can you go on to the next morning and what happened then, please?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "We were woken up by the head of the household and we had coffee and plum brandy. Before half past four and five o'clock, we heard the first large explosion, and then five, ten minutes later, another one. So then the head of the household told us that the first bridge that had been blown up was the bridge in the centre of Brcko which was connecting Brcko to Republic of Croatia, in fact, to the place called Gunja, and that the second explosion was at the railway bridge which was also connecting Brcko to Republic of Croatia, and we learned which formations had carried out the mining of the bridge."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Which formations were responsible for that?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The Red Berets."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I pause to offer to the Court and perhaps to the Defence cutting out that long answer from being read and to move straight on to the next question. Unless anybody wants the detail, it doesn't touch precisely on our topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the next question, please, putting a "blank" in for the name?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Did you see [blank] in Brcko?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No. I heard which were the places where he had gone to and who he met."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. You mentioned that you took with you from Bijelina a uniform. What uniform did you have?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Some people had ordinary olive grey and some people had camouflage but the reason is so that we would not be noticed, and when we arrived that's why our uniforms were in bags."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "What uniform did you have?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I had a camouflage. I had been given a camouflage uniform at the sugar processing plant."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "You did not have a uniform before you arrived there; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. Were you issued with a weapon at that time?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Now, I had a rifle from the Bijelina war and that I had received from [blank] who was the president of the Ledince local commune crisis staff. Now, at the same time, this is related to [blank], he was at three posts at the same time," and he then sets out the posts. He sets out the office of the same person at line 24. Line 26.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. Was that the only weapon that you had with you on the first day of May 1992?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "But at the sugar processing plant, they gave us extra ammunition and they gave us a bag with four extra ammunition sets for the automatic rifle. I had forgotten to say of course we were also given two hand grenades each to those who hadn't had them. Most people had something already, had either a hand grenade or handgun."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. Did you have a handgun?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. Were you given specific orders or instructions as to what you were to do on the first day of May 1992?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I was given specific instructions about the 3rd or 4th of May. I was at a checkpoint, that's what it was called, at the entrance to Srpska Varos on the railway, together with [blank] and an older man from Brcko. I think he'd been a teacher or something."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "What were you to do there?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "If we were told that if something arrived that was looking suspicious, a vehicle, that we should stop them, check the ID and search the car, nothing extra."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "On the 3rd or 4th of May, [blank] shot himself in the leg from the rifle and he was taken to the hospital, and the person who came for me to the checkpoint was [blank], presumably I think that's his name, [blank], being a nickname who was the chief of police in Bijelina. He put me in his official vehicle and took me to the police station in Brcko. He said he had a special task for me and that I mustn't fool around much and that I would be given direct instructions at the police station which had been liberated."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. What happened then?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I was brought to Brcko. I was taken to [blank]. There were some policemen there, some in uniforms, some in civilian clothes. They were inspectors of what, I don't know. I didn't know them then. I was then given a policeman's uniform, a scorpion handgun with a silencer, and I was given a Motorola. I was then given the nickname of Adolf by that very same chief and that I'm supposed to use that name, codename, for the Motorola. There was a group of young men from Bor who were all in black uniforms. There were those with the Red Berets and then there were these people from Serbian Volunteers Guard who had the Tigers insignia. Then there was the Bijelina police. Bijelina police were stationed at the Galeb Hotel, and it was on the 6th or 7th of May that the first murder happened."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. The meeting where you were taken to see [blank] was on the 3rd or 4th of May; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Yes. I'm not quite sure. A lot of time has passed."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Do you remember what day of the week it was?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No, I don't remember."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Was that the first time that you were given the name Adolf?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "What did he say to you at the time you were given that name?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "That that would be my code, that I was to use it for the Motorola."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Was that the first time that you used that nickname?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I don't understand the question."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Did you use the nickname Adolf at any time before the 3rd or 4th of May, 1992?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Who suggested the name Adolf?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "This man [blank] from Bijelina who gave me the Scorpio, who gave me the silencer, who gave me the Motorola."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Do you know why he chose the name Adolf?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I have no idea," and I don't propose to read the remainder of that answer unless it's wanted that I should do so. Mr. O'Donnell, if you could go to line 15 passage.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Were there other people with you at the time that you were given your uniform and pistol and the name?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Yes, it was a full station."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Do you know any of the other names that were given to people?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Then? At that time?"

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Yes, with you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No. I knew [blank]. I knew that other guy was [blank].

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "But were they given their names at the same time as you or did they already have those names?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "It must have been before. It wasn't then because when I arrived they had already been calling each other over Motorolas with their codes."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Was anything else said about the name Adolf when it was given to you?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No. I can't think of what could have been said, just to report on that name and that the Motorola at the station had to be on all the time."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Did they tell you that the name had any significance?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Just the code, just the code to answer."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Was there any reference made to Hitler or anyone else?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No. No. It was only later when people heard how they were calling me that everyone -- everybody started making jokes," and the interpreter interrupted and said, "So he said, 'I just needed a little moustache and that would be perfect.'"

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "What position did you hold with the Brcko police?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No position. No position. I had no position. I have completed eight grades of primary school. Even in the army when I served my military service, I did not have a rank, so. Of course, later on I was given the description of being the murderer for the SUP, for the police station."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Can you describe the uniform that you were given?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "It's a shirt, pale blue shirt that was the uniform of the former Yugoslav police," and I think we can turn on over the page, unless more detail is wanted. In summary, he deals with his uniform, Mr. O'Donnell, with his knowledge of ranks, and matters of that sort, and at the top of page 16, did he deal with the fact that he was provided also with a baton and with handcuffs?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He deals with the size of the scorpion pistol, but we have photographs of it and of the silencer, but he deals with that all in detail. If we go over to page 17, line 1, please.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. Please take your time and tell me whatever details you can as we go through. Firstly, Counts 6 and 7, it is alleged that on or about the 6th or 7th of May, 1992, you escorted an unknown male down the street near the Brcko police station where you shot him in the head with a scorpion pistol and killed him. What can you tell me about that matter?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I was told to go to have my baptism of fire. Blank, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we proceed in the same way and say, "[blank], [blank]", Mr. Londrovic, I think that would make it the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I seem to remember that the indictment was read publicly, if you recall. When Mr. Jelisic has had his initial appearance, it was read out. It's public. So I think that we should just take the precaution of putting in as many blanks, that is to say, wherever names occur, that that is sufficient. Please continue, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Your Honour, I hope that the speed that I'm going is neither too fast nor too slow. If the interpreters know that they have found their documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's rather fast than slow, if you want, because you are proceeding a little quickly perhaps. So try and slow down just a little bit, if you would. We're going to try and get this 4th of June interview done with, and we'll then have a pause. So we're going to try and take into account, as much as possible, the comments and remarks made by Mr. Londrovic regarding the accused's family. So with these reservations, I should like to ask you to continue, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Line 11: "[Blank] and myself, he had been leader of [blank], who had all been in black uniforms. We went down in front of the building and we met these two reporters or two photographers. We had been told by [blank] first that we would go and execute two civilians and that after that we were supposed to be photographed with a coffin in front of the police station, that we could then pretend that we were mourning this Serb," in inverted commas, "who had just been killed by Muslims. But the coffin was empty. There was nothing written on the cross. There were some wreathes. This was all a propaganda. It was all a setup. "From the infamous cell number 13, [blank] took out two prisoners from the police station. Whoever came to be in that cell number 13 had no chance whatsoever of surviving. These people had been on lists, and they had been tried and sentenced in advance. We took away these civilians towards the market centre down the street. I shot at one and [blank] shot at the other. I shot from the Scorpion pistol, and [blank] shot from his automatic rifle. "The only thing I can't remember is which uniform [blank] was wearing, but I think it might have well been also police uniform, but they must be on photographs. And these two photographers, [blank] and [blank], were standing at the side, and they were taking pictures as we were in different stages of us killing these two people. "When we finished that, we returned to the SUP building, and just opposite the SUP is a small park and there's a -- it's a small park just opposite. People from SUP had already organised the coffin, the wreathes and everything, but now we took a young woman called [blank] and we were -- we were -- this was all pretence. She was pretending. She was screaming in mourning for whoever had been killed and whoever -- and who was then in the coffin, so she was pretending to cry and so were we."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. I'll ask you a few questions about the shooting. "You said that you met with [blank], and before the shooting he told you that you would have your, as you put it, baptism by fire?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No, [blank] had said that I would have my baptism by fire, but [blank] had said that a lot of things had been screwed up in Brcko, and that things needed to be cleared up, and that we needed extra propaganda to show what was happening."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "When was the first time that you were told that those two people were going to be killed?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Repeated the question following an interjection by the interpreter, and at line 22, the defendant said: "[Blank] said that I would be going to my baptism by fire and that two people would be executed, and [blank] said -- said, 'Then give the reasons why.' And they thought that these two photographers, because they were Serbs, that they would be working for the Serbian cause. Of course, they had no idea that these photographs would end up with The Hague Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Was there anyone else in the room when the discussion took place about the executions?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Who else was in the room?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I don't -- I really don't know the names, but there must have been between 20 and 30 civilians. Among them was Amir Novalic, also known as Fric. I know, it's indictment, I know that he was called Fric."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Sorry. What I'm asking you is when there was a discussion about the executions and [blank] was talking about the propaganda that was needed, were there other people in that room?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "[Blank] and myself. We were called upstairs to be given instructions, [blank] and myself."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "You went downstairs to cell number 13 after that; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we can probably now move straight on by summarising the next page or so. He deals with matters then, in answer to your questions, in some details, I think, Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He sets out the history of how he took these two men and how they shot both of them, something that, as you know, is covered by some photographs that are going to be produced in evidence in this court?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 21, line 10?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "How many shots did you fire at the person that you killed?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I have no idea. Maybe two or three bullets. I don't want you to misunderstand me. I really, really don't remember these things. It's been a long time."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "I understand that a lot of questions that I ask you, you may -- you might have trouble recalling details. If that's the case, please tell me."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there's some then further matters of detail. If we go to page 22, you repeat substantially the account that he's been giving already; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 23 again fills out that account, and we can come to page 24. Having been asked about the body, did he, at the top of page 24, say this: "There were more bodies later on that accumulated there. I know, because I had been walking around town, and later on a small lorry came and piled up all these bodies, and I think they took them in the direction of Bijeljina, where the pit was. I don't think it was the Serbs who loaded these bodies onto the small lorry. It may have been Muslims, because there was a Muslim in front of police station who were cleaning the windows, especially cleaning the glass from the windows. That's the windows that had shattered during the explosions"?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I then went on to say: "Did you then leave the bodies where they fell or did you take them somewhere?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "We didn't carry them. I've never touched a corpse, a body."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Why did you shoot that man?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "As I was told to."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Do you believe that you had any justification for killing him?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "It's up to you to decide. I -- it's whether I had to, whether I was justified, whether I was told to. I don't know. I'm just telling you the way it was."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "What do you believe would have happened if you did not kill him?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I probably would be given a treatment by [blank]. I had had a taste of it before the war, and it probably would have been treatment in terms of possibly intimidation, some physical violence applied or something. But I am talking about [blank]. They knew very well about my sentence, three-and-a-half-year sentence, and they often put it out to threaten me."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Do you believe that you would have suffered some type of physical violence if you did not carry out the order?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Yes. I believe that I would have suffered some kind of punishment."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Was that mentioned to you at any time?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "When?"

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "At the time of being told to do this killing."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "After several murders that I committed, several crimes that I have committed, I have been given a kind of treatment by the intervention platoon, and the second time I -- when they wanted me -- to force me to do things, then I had -- and I shot, I fired from the same Scorpion into both my legs."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Were there any threats made to you before doing this killing?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "If I had protested, there would have been threats. But because I did not protest, there were no threats."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "And you think those threats would have taken the form of some sort of assault; is that right?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Perhaps beaten me up, locked me up, or returned me to Bijeljina to prison."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. Could you have left Brcko?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "When the last time when they were -- when I -- just before I had to fire into my legs when the federal SUP came to take me back to Brcko, that's when -- that's the special unit from the Yugoslav SUP, from the Federal Secretariat to the Interior of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and leadership ...", and then a name.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Prior to the meeting with [blank] and [blank], just before this killing, were you told at any time that you would have to kill people?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Could you have left Brcko on the 6th or 7th of May?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Well, there was not -- not really many checkpoints or anything. I suppose I could have been -- I could have just left, but I'm sure I would have been returned, just like I was returned from --" an unclear word. "There are non-Serbs that were in SUP and that were going to be executed by me, and I took these people who will come and testify for me that I took to another location and were not killed. You probably will have the opportunity to speak with these people."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then show the defendant photographs from the Washington Post, part of a sequence of photographs that are going to be shown as an exhibit in this case?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he identify himself as being the man in the photograph, killing, by shooting, the victim seen there?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He identifies the place -- we've had it in evidence -- and there was a break in the interview at the top of page 27?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interview continued, and at line 21 you moved on to counts 8 and 9, the killing of Hasan Jasarevic, who fled from the police station. Did you say to him: "What can you tell me about that incident?" He said, "Yes, I did it"; line 28?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct. I said, "What can you tell me about it?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "This murder is in -- related to the killing of Amir Novalic. If you don't mind, I would like to go to Novalic, to explain about Novalic, and then I can explain. It follows on how it happened about Hasan Jasarevic."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "If that's easier, that's no problem at all."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "It's related because, chronologically, Amir Novalic's murder happened first."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Sure, okay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "And then there was an escape and then this other one."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. For purposes of the tape, I'll put some details on tape and then you can continue with the murder of Amir Novalic. What we will talk about is counts 16 and 17. "It is alleged that on or about the 7th of May, 1992, you shot and killed a Muslim detainee named Amir Novalic, also known as Fric, inside the Brcko police station. What can you tell me about that matter?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Amir Novalic, also known as Fric, was being interrogated in a cell next-door, in a room next-door to the cell number 13. He was interrogated or, more precisely, said they were beating him up. He was beaten up by the members of the intervention platoon of the police. "At one point, a young man left that room. I was in the corridor of the police station. It's as you enter the police station, it's the corridor to the right. And then on the left-hand side, there were two bathrooms, then number 13 cell, the infamous, and then that office, that room where Amir Novalic, also known as Fric, was. "So from that point, a group of policemen came out. Some of them had blood on them, and what they said was, 'Go and have a look how we -- we've processed this guy.' I approached the room, and as I approached the cell, as I came to the door, Amir Novalic, completed covered in blood, completely beaten up, rushed towards me with an axe. As he was going to hit me with the axe, I started running away from him towards the other end of the corridor, and I couldn't shoot because on the other side of the corridor behind him there was a group of about 10 or 15 policemen, and they were standing there and watching what was going on. And I took -- I lifted a chair to protect myself from the axe, and so as I lifted it, he hit me on the arm, which is what I -- which is what I had it bandaged, which can be seen on that photograph. As I know I just wanted to defend him, I lifted it -- did not go towards him. I lifted the chair." Following an interjection by the interpreter: "And I started to run outside of the building towards the exit. Fric then lifted himself up, and he had the axe." Following an intervention, you said --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. You said he's run at you with the axe and you picked up a chair; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two answers further on, for substance. Line 11: "I lifted a chair like what I wanted to protect myself from the axe. I lifted it too much, and the axe hit me with the axe on my right hand, on the lower part of my right arm. I can explain later on about how the axe happened to be there. "And then when I turned back and a man from the formation Red Berets with the nickname [blank], he lives there now, and from the handgun he fired one shot in the direction of Fric. And as he hit him, as the bullet -- as he fired, Fric fell, and so we concluded that he had hit him. After Fric fell, [blank] approached with an automatic rifle, and he fired a round into the automatic rifle -- into the chest of Fric. I was in the corridor of the building and I was watching it all, and I remember that [blank] ran down the stairs, that he didn't even ask what had happened. He just started to complain, and loudly, why were people being killed inside the building. "Before I was taken to the hospital to have my arm bandaged, this man, Hasan Jasarevic, made a break free. He tried to escape from the building of the SUP, of the police station, with another young man, with another man. So one of them went towards the place where the first killing -- where the killings from counts 6 and 7 took place, towards that direction, and Hasan Jasarevic set off towards a small newspaper kiosk and the fountain there. There used to be a fountain there."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. Before we go on to that other count, I want to ask you some further questions about the killing of Fric."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 30, we can skip the questions about Fric and go to line 21. "Later on, we can go on to Jasarevic, but anyway after I had come back, or later on when I returned from the hospital, I asked who this man was, how courageous of him to have done what he had done, so I learned how Fric --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think -- how long do you intend to go on? Which page do you wish to cover before the break? I think it is time. This interview ends on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This interview goes to page 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite right. So we shall make a break then. We shall make a break and it will be a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The session is resumed. Will you have the accused brought in, please? Mr. Nice, before we resume -- no, we have to wait for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we resume, the Judges wondered about the method you used, concerned, on one hand, about not wasting time, on the other, to work, and we just wonder if this was really the best method to be applied. Because this binder was given to the Judges and, of course, they are familiar with it. Well, they are not particularly conversant with it, but they have it. On the other hand, the witness is here not only to give us his impressions but also to pinpoint the important points, which are said important points today. It seems to me that the important point is, on one hand, to highlight the most important elements relative the genocide, and I am not talking about what the accused has already admitted; and on the other hand, the witness told us that there were some contradictions, some inconsistencies, and we believe that he was to show us today which are these inconsistencies and contradictions. We have now been reading fragments of these interviews, which we do have before our eyes, and I believe that this debate is losing some of its transparency. I'm afraid that at the time of cross-examination, the Defence will then catch up those elements which the witness has not indicated or clarified, and then, of course, in your re-examination, you will be responding to that. So I wanted to mention this on behalf of my colleagues. What do you think about these concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I said at the beginning of the afternoon session, I thought it likely that we would develop a modus vivendi after the first passage of the interviews. It seemed important to me, and I trust that the Chamber may agree, to have that first passage of background which you haven't had before set out in some detail. But we've now reached a place where, as I forecast, we will be able to accelerate the speed with which we go through the material, and, indeed, I have marked the pages that touch on contradictions, as well as those that touch on counts. Subject to the technical difficulties that I must cope with that relate to the B/C/S booth, which I've heard about in the pause, I think we can make good progress. It may be that by the end of this afternoon's session, the Chamber would either be prepared to take the necessary balance of material read or to be read or be satisfied that I'm moving at such a speed that only a small part of tomorrow will be consumed with the interviews. I rather doubt if there's very much that Mr. Greaves wants to cross-examine on, because thus far I have been putting in the matters that he wanted to be put in, and I also know that he has himself, since he identified the passages he wanted to go in, taken the view that perhaps not all of that needs to be led. So I'm pretty confident that, one way or another, we will be able to speed up the process and complete the evidence in this case tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but may I remind you once again that on the counts which we have here, the accused has admitted and has pleaded guilty. So what I'm wondering is what is the purpose of this particular exercise? Do not, please, misunderstand me. This Chamber is not asking for the repetition for the sake of repetition, and I believe that we have already said that. We are not really here to organise a race, but we are here to conduct our work efficiently. If efficiency means that we have to be long, we shall be long. But it seems to me that we are long without being efficient, and that is my problem. I know the accused has pleaded guilty on so many counts, but we are here seeking the evidence of genocide. In this binder, you or, rather, your witness should indicate which are the elements which constitute genocide, you should draw our attention to those, or if it is to clarify perhaps the personality of the accused, those should be the primary concerns. That is all that I really am saying. Of course, you have to do your job, and go on as you wish, but will you please bear in mind those observations made by the Judges? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Those are the passages we have identified, and, indeed, of course, the killings to which he has pleaded guilty may be relevant where he sets out his mental process. But if you'll trust me, we can move from page 30 in the English, and I'm afraid I don't know the B/C/S page numbers, but if the B/C/S booth can let me know what page that is, I'll endeavour to overcome the technical problem that we've been having about page numbering.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We left off at page 20. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm going to go in the English version from page 30, Mr. O'Donnell, straight to page 34, which deals with the issue of how much thought he gave to a killing to which he may have pleaded guilty, but it's nevertheless important for that reason. On our page 34, shortly before the end of the first tape, at line 25, did you ask him: "Did you know Hasan Jasarevic before the shooting?"

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he replied, "No." Carry on.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I said, "Can you describe him for me?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Do you know what ethnicity he was?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Muslim."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Do you know anything about him?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Nothing."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Where he worked, where he lived, anything else?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Probably, he's probably from Brcko. He had been in the cell number 13 so he must have been something." That's the end of the first tape. In the English version, I turn over one page to page 36. Is it right, Mr. O'Donnell, that at line 24, you asked him if he said anything to Jasarevic before he shot him, and he said, "No, I don't think so. I think as soon as I ran out and I just shot, as they were holding him I shot ... We had no opportunity to exchange words. It just happened. He was, he was trying to escape."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct. I went on to say, "Do you recall him saying anything to you?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's my mistake. "I don't think so. His back was turned." That's all I need from that. If we turn on now to several pages, in the English version, we can turn on to page 47. Your Honours, I'll give the B/C/S booth some time to find the parallel page.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I direct your attention to the end of page 37, the beginning of 38, which I believe is important?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. English version, page 37, at the foot of the page, you asked him?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. Were you told to kill Hasan Jasarevic by anyone?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The answer: "I cannot say that anybody said to me, go and kill him now. It was just that he had, simply had tried to escape and I went after him, but he had been in the hands of this other, of these other soldiers."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "He was already captured at the time you shot him, is that right?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think he then just goes on to deal with more of that, but the essential point you wanted to cover is dealt with there. In the English version then, at page 47, and for the assistance of the Chamber, he picks up here with the list again and provides a few more details about the list of which he's spoken. At the foot of the page, in the middle of the page, you asked him, "Can you tell me about the list, can you describe the list to me, please?" He replies, "What was written was for instance the header was Serbia Police Station Brcko and then it was a list of Muslim prisoners. I can't remember what the description of the Muslims was. And it had at the end, it had Crisis Staff for, meaning for the Crisis Staff, and then signature of [blank] and his name printed."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "How many pages was the list?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "One. I think there were twenty-three, between twenty and twenty-five names, I think twenty-three names."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Was it typed or written?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he says it was typed, and on the following page, he gives further details. But at line 10, in particular, he says this on page 48 in the English version: "There were just one, two, three names. There was a 'one,' for instance, and then a name, and then in brackets it said Muslim. And all the people on my list were Muslims presumably if I had a Croat there would have been Croat." Is it right that he then set out that there were no other instructions, he said, that were given to him?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the page to page 49 in the English version, and starting at the foot of the page, is this one of the inconsistencies you wanted to draw to the Judges' attention?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting at line 36 on English page 49, please read on.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I said, "What did he tell you --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the B/C/S follow? I'm thinking about the accused. I'm thinking about the Defence. Can the B/C/S booth follow? Because, evidently, the page numbering is not the same.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: They are completely wrong. We can't find the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, I just got a big sign of negation, showing me they could not really keep up with you, and I'm thinking of the accused and the Defence and Mr. Londrovic. Perhaps it is too fast for them. I don't know. Some people say that I'm very fast, but sometimes I'm fast. The French booth, how about them? Can we go on? Will it be all right now? Proceed, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 49, line 36, the question?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "What did he tell you had to do with the people on the list?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "That I was supposed to kill them. With the list, that's how I made mistakes. I was taken to Laser. They took me from the police station because I don't know where -- I don't know where Laser was."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "I still need to get some more details about the conversation with [blank]. Do you remember exactly what he said to you about what you were to do in relation to the killing?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Here's a list of balijas, Ustashas, here it is and it had a signature." And in B/C/S, this is on page 34, Mr. Tochilovsky helpfully tells me. I'm at line 10 in the English version, and I continue. " The [blank] was there. He asked me whether I had been inside the number 13 cell. I had, yes, I had been inside. I couldn't say that I didn't go, because I had been. I wanted to see who was in there. And the key from cell number 13 was with the duty officer who was there, and he also had a hole through which we could check what was going on inside. Perhaps it was this size. Up to about halfway, it's empty, and then from about halfway, there is some kind of wooden bench or something. So it's kind of a wide bench about that high on which these people were sitting. They had no blankets or anything like that. I saw, when I went in, they used their jackets under their heads."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay. So you said he asked you if you had been into cell 13. What was said after that?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I can't quite remember the details. What he may have done then, I think he may have done, is just then given me the list and said, 'Well, here they are. You've got them downstairs, you've got them in Laser, you've got them in Luka.' I had never heard, until then, about Luka. I think Luka may have been formed around the 7th or something, because Luka was formed after they got people out of Laser, where they had kept them until then."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Yes, but what did he say about actually killing them?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then over the page, we skip a couple of questions and answers. He returns to say, at line 8 in the English?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "You said that you were told that it was going to be your baptism by fire and that you were told to kill those people?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you asked him a further slightly longer question, and at line 18, he said, in the English: "The lists were probably held. I'll tell you how it went. These were lists for executions, and the lists were probably held by people who had been interrogating them. For example, they sent me to detain Kemal Sulejmanovic. After the interrogators had spoken to him, if the order was to kill him, I would kill him." Page 35 in the B/C/S. "And then, of course, if they had the orders to continue his detention or to return him to detention, then that would continue. Nothing would happen to him. I think you will understand that through the murder of Naza Bukvic and her father."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Okay".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You asked him another question. He said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please try not to use the names, not to read out the names? Will you please just tell us "blank"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've only been reading out the names of the identified victims, I think, that have already been given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at line 30 in the English, he continued: "He didn't say 'kill', he didn't say 'kill'. He said, 'Here is a list of people who have to be liquidated.' As long as there was his signature in the name of [blank], that means that somebody somewhere had decided this, and I know. I learned later on who was deciding what in the [blank]. For instance, the person responsible for --" And then he gives a number of names which we needn't deal with. You asked him, in page 52 of the English, line 5, another question. He went on, asked if he had been surprised: "Well, I wasn't at all pleased that I would have to kill people. I thought it was just going to be a policeman, like before, but I think I took it all very lightly. I couldn't imagine that a person who got eight grades of school and who was supposed to go to sit a sentence in gaol, that I would then be -- have this power. We'll have a non-Serb witness, whom I was told to liquidate, whom I took to a certain location and left there. At that time, I was risking my own life, and the specific case was ..." And he then gives a job position. " ... and he was not on my list." If we turn over to page 53, in the middle of the page, Mr. O'Donnell, is there a passage that you want to draw particularly to the Court's attention?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: There is. It starts with the question: "Did you question your order to kill these people?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's line 21. Answer: "Well, I wasn't indifferent to that." Carry on.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "What do you mean by that?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "It was not pleasant to be given this list and being told to kill people. These people were never given a chance to defend themselves. They were completely helpless."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Well, that's why I'm asking the question. It seems completely strange that you would be given a list of people to kill and not question that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I had -- I had no -- there was no way that I could have questioned it. It was war. It was not a game. There was nobody that I could appeal to. There was nobody that I could protest to."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: "Did you protest or question any of the lists that you were given?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He then says, "No, to be honest." At the foot of that page, he starts off with a long answer that again you want to draw to the Court's attention, I think.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This relates to which topic, the one at the bottom of the page that you think is significant?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It relates to whether or not he was able to leave Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whether he had the freedom of movement that he subsequently denied having?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can deal with this one, I think, in summary. There's a long answer at English page 54, B/C/S page 37, where he speaks of a particular post holder and sets out how it was that he was able to drive this man. Just tell us where, please, Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: He was able to take him to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can then, unless you particularly want to draw our attention to anything else, can go to page 57 in the English, where he claims at line 5, in a long answer -- and it's B/C/S page 39 at the top -- he claims that he spared the life of a Dr. Ramic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
